title: String Transforms Into Another String
statement:
You are given two strings `str1` and `str2` of the same length, both made of lowercase English letters. A **conversion** picks one letter and rewrites every occurrence of it in `str1` as a single other lowercase English letter of your choice. Conversions apply to the string as it is after the earlier ones.

Return `true` if some sequence of zero or more conversions turns `str1` into exactly `str2`, and `false` if none does.
constraints: str1 and str2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

A conversion moves every copy of a letter together, and once two letters have been merged they can never be told apart again. So every letter of `str1` must always line up with **one** letter of `str2`; if some letter would need two different targets, the answer is `false`.

If the mapping is consistent, the only obstacle is order. A chain like `a -> c`, `c -> e` is done back to front (`c` first). A cycle such as `a -> b`, `b -> a` needs a spare letter as a temporary: `a -> z`, `b -> a`, `z -> b`. A spare letter exists whenever `str2` uses fewer than 26 letters: either `str1` misses some letter, or `str1` uses all 26 while two of them share a target, and merging those two first frees one. When `str2` uses all 26 letters, the mapping is a permutation and the very first conversion would merge two letters with different targets, so only `str1 === str2` works.

## Approach

1. If the strings are already equal, return `true` (zero conversions).
2. Walk both strings together and store `mapping.set(from, to)`; if `from` already maps to a different letter, return `false`.
3. Put the letters of `str2` in a set `targets`.
4. Return whether `targets.size < 26`, meaning a spare letter is available.

## Example 1, step by step

`str1 = "aabcc"`, `str2 = "ccdee"`. The strings differ. The walk records `a -> c` twice, `b -> d`, and `c -> e` twice, with no conflict. `targets` is `{c, d, e}`, only 3 letters, so the answer is `true`: convert `c` to `e`, then `b` to `d`, then `a` to `c`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the strings plus building a set of at most 26 letters.
- Space: O(1): the map and the set never hold more than 26 entries.

## Pitfalls

- Check `str1 === str2` first: a full-alphabet string can be "converted" into itself.
- The test is on the letters of `str2`, not `str1`: `"abc...xyz"` to `"bcd...yzz"` uses 25 target letters and works.
- A one-to-many letter (`"aa"` to `"ab"`) is impossible, but many-to-one (`"ab"` to `"aa"`) is fine.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `mapping` | the target letter each letter of `str1` must become |
| `from`, `to` | the letters at position `i` of `str1` and `str2` |
| `targets` | the distinct letters used by `str2` |

narration.2: Equal strings need no conversion at all.
narration.6: mapping records which letter each letter of str1 has to become.
narration.7: Walk both strings position by position.
narration.8: The letter currently in str1 at this position...
narration.9: ...and the letter it must end up as.
narration.10: If this letter was already promised a different target, no conversion can split it.
narration.13: Record (or confirm) the target for this letter.
narration.16: Collect the distinct letters str2 uses.
narration.17: A consistent mapping is achievable exactly when a spare letter exists to break cycles.
